summary:
Firescope is a web tool for exploring 26 years (2000–2026) of satellite-detected fire hotspots in Italy. It harmonises MODIS and VIIRS data from NASA FIRMS into one comparable dataset, so users can view the whole country or draw a radius around any point to check local fire activity. Charts show weekly hotspot counts within a year or the same week across years, with separate lines for raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, and harmonised data.

MODIS and VIIRS have different resolutions (1 km vs 375 m) and detection sensitivities, so raw counts aren't directly comparable across years. Harmonising them makes long-term trends readable. This matters for anyone tracking fire patterns or how sensor changes affect what looks like fire activity.
details:
What it does and how it works

Firescope is a browser-based tool that visualises 26 years (2000–2026) of satellite fire hotspot data for Italy (chosen as test region). Users pick a year and an ISO week, or click any point on the map and set a radius, to see every hotspot detected in that window. A chart plots weekly hotspot counts either within a chosen year or for the same week across all years, with separate lines for raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, and harmonised data.

Behind the scenes, the data goes through a pipeline: each sensor's CSV is cleaned (non-vegetation fire types removed, low-confidence detections filtered), trimmed to five columns, and merged across sensors using a 1 km spatial buffer within the same UTC day.

Benefits and intended impact

MODIS (1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m) detect very different numbers of fires. Therefore comparing raw counts across years gives a misleading picture of fire activity. Harmonising them into a common framework makes long-term trends and seasonal patterns readable. The intended impact is to give researchers, journalists, and citizens a quick way to check whether fire activity in a given week or region is unusual, without needing GIS software or raw FIRMS downloads.

Tools and languages

  • Python for the data pipeline: csv and math from the standard library for filtering, merging, and aggregation; custom scripts for each stage (filter type, filter confidence, slim columns, cross-sensor merge, CSV→GeoJSON).
  • JavaScript with a map library for the front end, plus charts for the weekly series.
  • HTML/CSS for layout.
  • GitHub Pages for hosting; data files stored as GeoJSON and CSV.

Creativity

Most FIRMS-based tools show one sensor at a time or a single year. Firescope lets you hold the week constant and slide across 26 years, which makes the effect of sensor changes immediately visible — you can see the jump when VIIRS data starts. The radius tool also turns a national dataset into a local one without preprocessing.

Factors considered

  • Sensor comparability: harmonising MODIS and VIIRS was the central design problem; without it, any year-over-year comparison would be misleading.
  • Data provenance: the interface shows raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, and harmonised counts side by side, so users can see what harmonisation changed rather than trusting a single number.
  • Accessibility: no installation, no login, no GIS knowledge required.
